notes.title: Power Plant and Engine Control
notes.subtitle: The Arriel 2D — a 700 kW-class engine in the same airframe as the 2B1 — its dual-channel FADEC governing N2, the automatic second-chance start, and the EBCAU back-up governor holding N2 388–400 rpm after a total FADEC failure.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.7 (Power Plant — General, Engine Oil System), Section 7.8 §5 (Fuel Flow Control — FADEC functions, N2 governing, FADEC failures, Fuel governor back-up system, Automatic 2nd chance engine start), and Section 7.1 §2 (Descriptive Data — engine ratings).

sections.heading: The engine
paragraphs: A single Turbomeca (Safran) Arriel 2D, a 700 kW (937 SHP) class turboshaft, in its own fireproof compartment aft of the MGB and above the rear cargo hold, connected to the MGB by a shaft between two flexible couplings. Maximum take-off power (MTOP) is 641 kW (860 SHP); maximum continuous power (MCP) is 551 kW (739 SHP) — meaningfully more installed power than the 2B1 in the same airframe.

It is a modular free-wheel engine of five independent modules: an accessory drive gearbox / transmission shaft, an axial compressor, a gas generator HP section, a power turbine, and a reduction gearbox. The oil system is in two parts — an external system in the engine and MGB compartments with one tank and one cooler (fireproof hoses in the engine bay), and an internal system inside the engine with one pressure pump, three scavenge pumps, a filter with a by-pass valve, and one electrical magnetic chip detector.

sections.heading: The FADEC
paragraphs: Fuel flow is managed by a FADEC built around a dual-channel Electronic Engine Control Unit (EECU) in the rear cargo bay. It holds power turbine speed N2 constant regardless of the power drawn, by adjusting gas generator speed N1, metering fuel through a stepper motor on a valve in the engine's hydro-mechanical unit (HMU). At every engine start the FADEC automatically swaps which channel — A or B — drives the HMU, to expose any dormant failure.

The EECU also handles automatic starting with TOT overlimit prevention, proportional-integral N2 control, surge and flame-out protection during transients, bleed-valve monitoring, N1/TOT/torque overlimit protection, failure detection and indication, the Engine Health Check, and usage/N1/N2 cycle counting. Post-MOD 07-4831/07-20015 it adds automatic engine shutdown on an N2 overspeed above 120% (463 rpm) — the FADEC fires the engine stop electrovalve, cutting fuel for an immediate shutdown; restart capability is unaffected, and the function self-tests at every start (a detected failure flashes GOV).

sections.heading: N2 governing
paragraphs: The FADEC stabilises N2 on an N2 datum (N2*) sent from the VEMD over the crosstalk link. If that datum is not received, the FADEC reverts to an N2 of 394 rpm (NR equivalent) and GOV comes on. If the FADEC detects autorotation or a very low power setting, it automatically raises N2 in FLIGHT mode to about 400 rpm, to sharpen engine response and reduce the NR droop after a fast power demand.

Once gas generator speed is established (N1 > 60%), normal engine running is independent of the helicopter electrical system — the FADEC is then fed by a gas-generator-driven alternator with two independent channels. Helicopter 28 VDC is still needed for the starting sequence and monitoring, and as a back-up source for the EECU fuel control section.

sections.heading: The EBCAU back-up governor and automatic restart
paragraphs: The fuel governor back-up system is an electronic computer — the Engine Back-up Control Ancillary Unit (EBCAU) — completely independent of the FADEC. On detection of a total FADEC failure it takes over fuel governing immediately, holding N2 between 388 and 400 rpm through a DC actuator on a back-up metering valve whose slots sit partly in series and partly in parallel with the HMU's main metering valve, adding or subtracting fuel relative to the flow the frozen FADEC valve is still passing. Whenever the FADEC works, the back-up valve is held in neutral as a safety device.

During start, if ignition has not occurred 5 seconds after N1 passes 17%, the EECU stops the sequence on its own, lets N1 fall back to 10%, and then launches a fresh start sequence — a second-chance start managed entirely by the EECU with no pilot action.
sections.note: In-flight engine power reduction using the twist grip is prohibited except for engine failure training and the emergency procedures that call for it. Heating and demisting must not be used above the engine maximum continuous rating.

notes.title: Fuel System
notes.subtitle: A single spin-moulded (or crash-resistant) tank of roughly 425 kg usable, a priming pump used only for the start, and an engine side that heats the fuel enough to run at −20°C with no anti-ice additive.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.8 (Fuel System — General, Helicopter Supply System, Engine Fuel Supply System, Controls and Monitoring); Section 7.1 §2 (fuel capacity); Section 2.5 (approved fuels).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: The fuel system has a helicopter part and an engine part. The helicopter part is a spin-moulded tank (or a crash-resistant tank on modified aircraft), a supply system, a gravity refuelling filler, and a monitoring system. The engine part — an LP pump, a fuel filter, an HP pump, and the fuel-control hydro-mechanical unit — is integral with the engine, and the hydro-mechanical unit is driven by the FADEC and its back-up system.
Total capacity is 540 litres (427 kg); usable fuel with the crash-resistant tank is 538 litres / 425 kg (937 lb).

sections.heading: Helicopter supply side
paragraphs: The tank sits in the body structure beneath the transmission deck, with a fuel level transmitter, a priming pump, and a decanting sump with a water drain valve. A vent is on the right side, the filler on the left. Fuel reaches the engine through a fuel shut-off valve. The priming pump only primes the fuel line for starting — the engine draws its fuel by suction in normal running.

sections.heading: Engine supply side
paragraphs: The engine LP pump draws fuel through the filter to the HP pump. The filter carries a by-pass, a pressure transmitter, and a pressure/temperature transmitter that together determine the pre-clogging level. The fuel is warmed by the combined fuel/oil heat exchanger on the oil filter assembly — enough to allow operation down to −20°C with no anti-ice additive in the fuel — then delivered to the FADEC hydro-mechanical unit.

From there the fuel passes a shut-off solenoid valve (the means of shutting the engine down) and a pressurizing valve before reaching the main injector and injection wheel. A three-way electrovalve feeds two starting injectors during the start; once the start ends they are fed with P3 air to prevent carbonisation. On shutdown a purge valve drains the fuel left in the main injection system.

sections.heading: Controls and monitoring
paragraphs: The FUEL PUMP (FUEL P) indicator light shows the priming pump state — selected ON for start and purge, OFF once the engine is running. An engine fuel control back-up system (see the Power Plant note) can meter fuel through a back-up valve if the FADEC fails completely.
sections.note: If the fuel contains no freezing inhibitor and OAT is below −20°C, an anti-icing additive is mandatory. Only the fuels listed in Section 2.5 may be used.

notes.title: VEMD: Vehicle and Engine Management Display
notes.subtitle: A duplex display with two independent processing lanes, three operating modes, an FLI that shows the closest limit — and a Performance page whose weight entry also drives the LIMIT light.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.4 (VEMD — General, Characteristics, Operating Modes, Controls, Operation, Operational Mode pages, N2 Datum); Section 2.4 §3 (First Limitation Indicator); Section 4.3 (weight data entry).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: The VEMD is a duplex indicator with two matrix liquid-crystal displays in the centre of the instrument panel. It shows all the engine and vehicle parameters. It is built from three modules: two processing modules, LANE 1 and LANE 2, and one display module holding both screens and the control pushbuttons. It runs on a dual 28 VDC supply protected by circuit breakers.

It powers up automatically when the battery switch is turned on and runs an initialisation test of both lanes. Pressing OFF1 or OFF2 during the test cuts the chosen lane, validates the test and leaves the other lane in operation. After a successful test it goes to OPERATIONAL mode.

sections.heading: The pages
paragraphs: The FLI page tracks N1, TOT and torque together, so one indication shows whichever is closest to its limit. If one of the three becomes invalid the ENGINE page is displayed automatically and the parameters are read on independent scales. The VEMD upper screen switches to the FLI automatically when N1 passes 60 % during start.

The Engine Power Check runs in three phases — an initial stabilisation phase, a more restrictive stabilisation phase and a margin-computation phase. The result page shows N1, N2, TOT, pressure altitude, TRQ and OAT together with the torque margin against TOT and against N1, each positive or negative.

At the end of a flight (N1 below 10 % and NR below 70 rpm) the FLIGHT REPORT page appears automatically on the lower screen: flight number, flight time (from N1 above 60 % after start to N1 below 50 % at shutdown), usage counter, N1 and N2 cycles for the flight and in total, and a yellow message area if a discrepancy was detected.

sections.heading: The Performance page
paragraphs: The Performance page calculates aircraft weight and hover performance in and out of ground effect, with wind from any direction and — post MOD 07-5102 — with a headwind or no wind. The crew enters the equipped empty weight (it keeps the value from the previous flight and must be updated after any configuration change), the crew weight (default 80 kg / 176 lb at power-up) and the payload (set at power-up to match the maximum internal takeoff weight). Fuel, sling load (post MOD 07-4716), pressure altitude and OAT are taken automatically. A weight penalty can be entered post MOD 07-5102, in CONFIGURATION mode only.

Performance values below the actual all-up weight are shown in yellow. For mission planning the pressure altitude and OAT can be changed; the OAT then follows the standard-atmosphere law, and the VEMD goes back to the actual values when the page changes.
sections.note: On single-hydraulics aircraft post MOD 07-20039 this page is not only for performance planning: the weight entered here is one of the inputs to the LIMIT light and its 285 Hz tone, which is why the pre-start and before-takeoff checks both ask for the weight data to be entered and validated.

sections.heading: The N2 datum
paragraphs: The VEMD computes the N2 datum (N2*) from the collective and yaw-pedal positions and sends it to the FADEC over the crosstalk link. Both processing modules compute it; if they disagree, or if one or both inputs are invalid, a back-up value is sent instead. The VEMD also limits how fast N2* can change, so NR and torque do not jump. Post MOD 07-4716, with a hook load of 150 kg or more, N2* is held at a constant 400 rpm regardless of collective and pedal position.

notes.title: Central Warning Panel and Ancillary Systems
notes.subtitle: Three ASU cards behind the caution and warning lights — one of which is part of the engine fuel back-up system, not just the annunciators.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.3 (Central Warning and Ancillary Systems — Description, Characteristics, Ancillary Systems, Overhead Panel).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: The Caution and Warning Panel (CWP) carries red warning lights for alarms that need immediate action and amber caution lights for alarms whose action can be delayed. Audio alarms are generated through the intercommunication system and are enabled when the HORN switch on the central console is ON. The panel runs on a dual 28 VDC supply protected by circuit breakers.
Post MOD 07-20112 or MOD 07-20228 the overhead panel also carries fault indicators for WACS (the wireless airborne communication system) and, if installed, the flight data recorder.

sections.heading: Three Ancillary Systems Unit (ASU) cards
paragraphs: The ancillary systems are three ASU cards. Between them they manage all audio warnings, some visual warnings and the processing of specific electrical signals, plus the engine fuel control back-up system. Each card has a dual 28 VDC supply and is protected by breakers.

rows: Manages a warning light; generates the audio high and low NR warnings; manages the other audio warnings — a Gong for red alarms and a continuous low tone for an MTOP overlimit

notes.title: Power Transmission System and Rotors
notes.subtitle: Four links from engine to tail rotor, a Starflex hub with no bearings, and one reference speed — NR 386 rpm — that every engine and torque number is written against.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.9 (Power Transmission and Rotors); Section 2.4 (Vehicle Limitations); Section 5.1 §10 (glide distance in autorotation).

sections.heading: Engine to MGB
paragraphs: The transmission is a chain of four parts: the engine-to-MGB coupling, the main gearbox (MGB), the tail rotor drive shaft and the tail gearbox (TGB). The coupling is a drive shaft joining engine and MGB through a flexible coupling at each end, surrounded by a coupling tube, with a casing to the MGB and a gimbal ring between casing and tube.

sections.heading: The main gearbox
paragraphs: The MGB reduces speed from engine to main rotor, drives and supports the hydraulic pump, the MGB lubricating pump and the rotor brake, and carries the servo-control and suspension-bar attachment fittings. It is made of three interchangeable modules with its own lubrication, monitoring and maintenance access. The lubricating pump takes oil from the sump through a strainer, through an oil cooler and a filter, and the oil returns to the sump by gravity.

sections.heading: Tail rotor drive train
paragraphs: The tail rotor drive shaft is a forward steel shaft and a long light-alloy shaft, joined to each other, to the engine and to the TGB by three flexible couplings. The long shaft runs on five ball-bearing supports mounted on elastomeric bushes that damp vibration. The TGB sits at the end of the tail boom, combining power transmission and pitch control in one casing. It is splash-lubricated, with a visual oil-level indicator and a chip detector that lights TGB CHIP.

sections.heading: Rotors
paragraphs: The main rotor is semi-rigid with a Starflex hub that has no ball bearings and no lubrication system. It has three flexible glass-resin blades and turns clockwise seen from above. Flapping is taken by the composite star arms; lead-lag and pitch come from distortion of elastomeric parts. The tail rotor has two blades on a see-saw mount on the TGB and turns counter-clockwise seen from the right side.

notes.title: Hydraulic System
notes.subtitle: One pump, one circuit, accumulators that buy a limited time — and a LIMIT light whose accuracy depends on a weight you typed into the VEMD.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.10 (Hydraulic System — General, System Description, Normal Operation, Abnormal Operation); Section 2.3 §6 (maneuvering limitations); Section 3.6 (hydraulic failure); SUP.23 (dual hydraulic system).

sections.heading: The system
paragraphs: The hydraulics reduce collective, cyclic and pedal forces. Three main rotor servos (one longitudinal, two lateral) and a tail rotor servo do the work. Total fluid volume is 3 litres (0.79 US gal) to the maximum mark on the reservoir, which sits on top of the MGB.

A single constant-flow gear pump, belt-driven from a pulley on the engine power drive shaft near the MGB input, generates the pressure. The regulator unit holds a pressure regulating valve set to 40 bar (580 psi) pre-MOD 07-20039 or 60 bar (870 psi) post-MOD 07-20039, a pressure switch, a 3-micron filter with a clogging indicator and a solenoid electrovalve.

sections.heading: Safety units and the load compensator
paragraphs: Each main rotor servo carries a safety unit — an accumulator, a non-return valve and a solenoid electrovalve — that keeps hydraulic assistance for a limited time after pressure is lost, long enough to reach a flight regime where the loads are acceptable.

The yaw side is different. A load-compensating system (accumulator, non-return valve, pressure relief valve, pressure-drop solenoid electrovalve and actuator) reduces the yaw-pedal loads for an indefinite period after pressure is lost. Its pressure can only be dumped by selecting the accumulator test switch to TEST.

rows: Hydraulic cut-off switch (collective grip, guarded, ON/OFF)
OFF depressurises the system and, at the same time, the accumulators of the three main rotor servos; the tail rotor load compensator keeps its assist

TEST opens the regulator solenoid to depressurise the system and also opens the tail rotor servo solenoid, dumping the load compensator, while the main rotor servos run on their accumulators for a limited time

sections.heading: Cautions
paragraphs: HYDR on the CWP means loss of pressure or low pressure, with a single gong. Post MOD 07-20039, operating close to servo-transparency also lights LIMIT on the CWP with a continuous 285 Hz tone. The trigger is computed from weight (as entered on the VEMD Performance page), altitude, OAT, airspeed and load factor. The RFM warns that LIMIT and the tone must not be relied on as the sole means of avoiding servo-transparency.

sections.heading: Servo types
paragraphs: The aircraft can carry SAMM or Dunlop main rotor servos. SAMM servos have an input-play locking system; if the two lateral servos unlock at slightly different pressures during pressurisation, the cyclic can jump to one side — about 5 daN (11 lbf) of hold force with hand and knees prevents it. Dunlop lateral servos have no such device and are not subject to that asymmetric switch-over.

sections.heading: Pre-flight tests
paragraphs: Two tests are normal procedure before every flight. The ACCU TST test checks the accumulators still assist (HYDR flashes and the gong sounds). The cut-off test checks the dump valves; when the switch is returned to ON and ACCU TST to OFF, the time for pressure to recover is the check on nitrogen charge. It normally takes 3 to 4 seconds; 1 second or more than 4 seconds means at least one accumulator is faulty and maintenance is required before flight.

sections.heading: Abnormal operation — hydraulic pressure loss
paragraphs: Bank below 30° and no abrupt manoeuvres, then smoothly set IAS between 40 and 60 kt (74–111 km/h). From VNE or the hover this takes under 30 seconds on properly serviced accumulators. If control loads are felt earlier, set the cut-off switch OFF immediately; otherwise switch it OFF as soon as the safety speed is reached, even if assistance remains, so the three main accumulators depressurise together and the lateral loads stay symmetric.

At the safety speed with the collective near neutral (about 40 % torque) the pilot holds roughly 4 daN (9 lbf) left cyclic and 5 daN (11 lbf) forward cyclic, with near-zero collective force. In the hover, forces up to 5 daN (11 lbf) change direction quickly, which is why the RFM says not to hover or manoeuvre at low speed. Land from a flat approach with a slight running landing at about 10 kt (19 km/h), where up to 17 daN (38 lbf) of forward cyclic may be needed for less than 30 seconds.

sections.heading: Dual hydraulic system (SUP.23, optional)
paragraphs: With the dual system the panel shows HYD1 (left circuit) or HYD2 (right circuit) with SERVO for loss of pressure on one circuit; one remaining circuit allows continued safe flight and landing. Bank below 30° and IAS below 110 kt (204 km/h) or VNE if less. HYD2 also means tail rotor hydraulic power is lost and the ACCU TST button must not be pressed. SERVO alone is a jam of a distributor valve on the main servo unit. LIMIT alone means the main servo unit maximum load is reached; reduce power, speed or load factor and continue the flight. Do not exceed a load factor that lights LIMIT.

notes.title: Electrical Power Systems
notes.subtitle: A 28 VDC network built around the Electrical Master Box, a 150 A starter generator (200 A optional), and an optional AC side whose failure takes the AFCS with it.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.11 (Electrical Power Systems — DC and AC); Section 2.4 §6 (electrical circuit limitations); SUP.16 §3.8 (AFCS and electrical failures); SUP.29 (200 A starter generator).

sections.heading: DC power sources
paragraphs: The generating and distribution system supplies the network with regulated 28 VDC. The sources are a starter generator on the engine accessory gearbox, a 15 Ah battery in the right rear cargo bay (a second battery is optional) and a 28 V external power receptacle on the right side.

sections.heading: The Electrical Master Box
paragraphs: All three sources connect to the Electrical Master Box (EMB) in the rear cargo bay. It regulates the starter generator, connects the sources to the network through line contactors, distributes and protects the network against supply failures, and interfaces the generation and distribution system with the indicating, control and monitoring system. The distribution has a direct battery bus-bar (PP25), a primary bus-bar (PP12 in the EMB) and secondary bus-bars (PP5, PP6, PP9 and others), with cockpit and cargo-compartment breaker panels.

rows: 150 A with the basic starter generator
200 A unit (SUP.29) replaces the basic 150 A unit and gives increased electrical capacity; the 200 A limit applies when it is installed

sections.heading: AC power — optional
paragraphs: The AC system is fitted when the aircraft has an autopilot, gyroscopic instruments or other equipment that needs it. A static inverter, fed from DC, supplies it. Two systems exist: a 250 VA system (115 VAC 150 VA plus 26 VAC 150 VA, maximum 250 VA in total) and a 10 VA system (26 VAC 10 VA), both at 400 Hz. The inverter is fed from the PP9 bus through a 10 A protection for the 250 VA system or 2.5 A for the 10 VA system, switched on with the INV pushbutton, and an INV caution light shows the inverter is off or the AC system has failed.

sections.heading: What failure costs
paragraphs: With the SFIM AFCS fitted, an AC power failure disengages the AFCS automatically (hands on the controls, check INV ON and press it back on if needed). On total loss of electrical power the AFCS disengages automatically and cannot be re-engaged.

notes.title: AFCS: SFIM 85 T 31 (3-Axis)
notes.subtitle: An optional three-axis autopilot with a monitoring unit that disengages the faulty channel — and one hard rule for total electrical failure.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual SUP.16 (Automatic Flight Control System SFIM 85 T 31 — Description, Limitations, Emergency Procedures, Normal Procedures).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: The AFCS holds the attitudes (pitch, roll, yaw) and heading set by the pilot. Additional modes are A/S (holds present airspeed), ALT (holds present pressure altitude), HDG (acquires and holds the heading selected on the HSI) and T/C (automatic yaw and roll co-ordination in turns). The computer is linked to a vertical gyro, the HSI, a directional gyro and flux valve, an air data unit, a yaw-pedal displacement detector and a lateral accelerometer.

It has three series actuators (one per channel, each with a galvanometer and a channel-disengaged light) and two parallel trim actuators on pitch and roll with the artificial-load release (trim release) function. A failure monitoring unit compares the vertical gyro with the gyro horizon and warns and disengages the faulty channel; it switches on automatically as soon as a pitch or roll channel is engaged. AC comes from a static inverter (115 and 26 VAC, 400 Hz).

sections.heading: Limitations
paragraphs: On the ground the AFCS must be disengaged unless checks are being made, and it must not be engaged before takeoff if the trim test is not satisfactory. The minimum height for hands-off AFCS operation is 400 ft (120 m).

notes.title: Ventilation, Heating and Demisting
notes.subtitle: Two ventilation circuits, and a heating system that runs on engine P2 bleed air — which is why it is limited by engine power.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual Section 7.13 (Ventilation, Heating and Demisting); Section 2.4 §2 (takeoff power and heating).

sections.heading: Ventilation
paragraphs: Two separate circuits ventilate the cabin. Front ventilation takes air from the front cabin through two ducts to the crew, controlled by a pull-knob on the instrument panel. Overhead ventilation takes air from the upper cabin through a ram-air scoop to outlets in the structure posts; each outlet is opened and aimed individually.

sections.heading: Heating and demisting
paragraphs: Heating and demisting mix hot P2 air bled from the engine with outside air drawn from under the cabin floor. The mixture goes through two ducts to heating outlets under the front seats and to demisting manifolds at the bottom of the front windscreen. Two manually operated valves on the P2 lines, on the cabin floor, open and control warm-air distribution.

Because it takes engine bleed air, its use is tied to engine power: heating and demisting are authorised up to maximum takeoff power (TOP) in the basic manual. With the optional sand filter, heating and demisting must be off whenever P2 is ON.

notes.title: Sand Filter
notes.subtitle: A separator-tube filter on the engine intake, blown clear by P2 air — and the only way to fly in falling snow.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual SUP.14 (Sand Filter — General, Limitations, Emergency Procedures, Normal Procedures, Performance Data); Section 2.1 (forbidden operations).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: The sand filter protects the engine from sand ingestion in the hover or in sand-laden air, and also protects the intake from snow ingestion in falling snow. It has a filter on the engine air intake below the ice protection screen, a P2 air pressure supply system and an electrical control and monitoring system. Ambient air flows through separator tubes that form the filter; the sand leaves through scavenge tubes ventilated by P2 air.

The SAND FILT pushbutton on the console feeds an electric valve that opens and closes the P2 circuit. A P2 message on the VEMD FLI display shows the valve is fully open; the circuit is protected by the SAND FILT breaker.

sections.heading: Limitations
paragraphs: Heating and demisting must be off when P2 is ON. P2 must be OFF in visible moisture with OAT below 0 °C. Flight in falling snow is permitted with P2 OFF — and the basic manual forbids flight in falling snow without the sand filter installed.

sections.heading: Valve failure logic
paragraphs: If the P2 valve fails to open (P2 stays off), avoid flying in a sandy atmosphere. If it fails to close (P2 stays on), continue the flight while observing the P2 bleed-air limitations.

sections.heading: Operating notes
paragraphs: Before start, the exterior check includes the engine air intake and sand filter: no foreign objects, no ice or snow accumulations in or around the intake and no stagnant water at the drain hole — ice or snow left in or around the intake can be ingested and cause a sudden in-flight engine failure. The SAND FILT switch is tested ON and OFF before starting (P2 on the VEMD). For the engine health check the SAND FILT is OFF; the FADEC takes the filter into account automatically.

notes.title: Emergency Floatation Gear
notes.subtitle: Floats to keep the helicopter upright for an evacuation after an emergency landing on water — not a ditching certification.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual SUP.17 (Emergency Floatation Gear AERAZUR — General, Limitations, Emergency Procedures, Normal Procedures, Performance Data).

sections.heading: What it is — and what it isn't
paragraphs: The gear is approved for emergency use, not for ditching to JAR 27. It exists to keep the rotorcraft sufficiently upright and in adequate trim for a safe and orderly evacuation after an emergency landing on water. It consists of two floatation units along each skid, an inflation system with two cylinders (one per float, each with a pressure indicator), a FLOAT ARM pushbutton on the console or instrument panel, and a guarded FLOAT FIRE pushbutton on the collective grip.

sections.heading: Inflation
paragraphs: If float inflation is not possible with FLOAT ARM set to arm, continue the flight and stay within gliding distance of land. Inflation is not possible when the EMER SW is OFF or the battery switch is in EMER SHED.

To inflate, after an engine failure or another urgent need to alight on water and after checking rotor speed: FLOAT ARM ON, check FLOAT ARM lights 1 and 2 (at least one ON), then press FLOAT FIRE under its guard. The recommended firing speed is below 80 kt (148 km/h); above 80 KIAS a deceleration with a pitch-down movement can occur.

sections.heading: Autorotation onto water
paragraphs: Reduce collective to hold NR in the normal range and fly Vy. If a relight is impossible or after tail rotor failure, put the engine starting selector OFF, and head the aircraft equally between wind and wave direction on final. At about 70 ft (21 m) flare; at 20–25 ft (6–8 m) at constant attitude gradually raise the collective, then move the cyclic slightly forward for a 10° nose-up attitude and under 10 kt (19 km/h) at touchdown, cancelling any sideslip with the pedals and cushioning with the collective. After touchdown lower the collective fully, apply the rotor brake and evacuate once the rotor has stopped. When afloat the forward doors must be opened with the jettison handles.

sections.heading: Checks and performance
paragraphs: The exterior check confirms the floatation units are locked in the lowered position, the protective covers are in good condition and the pressure in both cylinders is within the placard limits; the interior check arms the system and confirms both FLOAT ARM lights ON. Stability after an emergency landing on water was demonstrated up to a significant wave height of 2.5 m (sea state 4). Rate of climb at Vy is reduced by 50 ft/min (0.25 m/s) and cruise speed by about 2 kt (3.7 km/h).

notes.title: Hoist Installation
notes.subtitle: A fixed-speed 136 kg hoist and a variable-speed 204 kg hoist — same crew rules, very different cable systems and duty limits.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual SUP.18 (Breeze / Air Equipment electric hoist 136 kg) and SUP.19 (Breeze electric hoist 204 kg); SUP.19.1 (204 kg hoist, grip with support bracket) is a further variant not covered here.

sections.heading: Two hoist families
paragraphs: Both installations raise or lower loads in the hover using a pivoting jib on the port side with a locking device for the ferrying and hoisting positions, a safety belt for the hoist operator, two cable protectors on the LH skid, a hand cable cutter stowed on the rear wall and a pyrotechnic cable cutter.

rows: Breeze BL 16600 or Air Equipment 76370, constant-speed electric motor
33.5 m (110 ft) Breeze; 40 m (130 ft) Air Equipment
Rocker switch on the control grip to raise, lower or stop
Thumbwheel on the grip — cable speed proportional to displacement — plus a cable-out indicator in metres
Up-limit switch-off; power cut with 4 m of cable left; mechanical pin stops the drum at 3 m if the down-limit fails
Electronic control unit decelerates automatically before the limits and stops at them, and on incorrect winding
100 A fuse in the EMB, 60 A breaker, two 2.5 A cutter breakers, 2.5 A up-down breaker
130 A fuse in the EMB, two 7.5 A cutter breakers, 100 A cut-off breaker, 2.5 A and 6.3 A control breakers

sections.heading: Crew and duty limits
paragraphs: The minimum crew is one pilot and one hoist operator, an experienced operator who wears a harness on a lanyard attached to the rear cabin panel — one person per attachment point, maximum 101 kg (222 lb) per point. Landing with a load suspended on the cable is prohibited, and a hand cable cutter must be within reach of the operator.

The 136 kg hoists have duty limits. Air Equipment: never more than 6 consecutive hoisting operations plus one descent with maximum load and maximum reel-out. Breeze: wait 30 seconds after each lowering or raising; after 3 complete cycles stopping the hoist for 40 minutes is recommended. The 204 kg supplement lists no such duty cycle.

sections.heading: Controls
paragraphs: The pilot switches the installation on with the HOIST pushbutton on the console and has a guarded cable-shear pushbutton on the collective grip. The operator has the control grip described above; on the 136 kg hoist a green light shows the hoist moving up and a red light is for the up-limit microswitch test.

sections.heading: Emergency procedures
paragraphs: Hoist failure: depending on load and circumstances, pull the cable in by hand, cut it, or return to base with the cable slightly inclined at a VNE of 60 kt (111 km/h). For a severely damaged cable, jam or miswrap, stop hoisting without using the speed control, inspect the cable, set the load down at the nearest suitable site, raise the cable by hand and store it in the cabin, switch HOIST OFF, and use the hand cutter if manual raising is not possible — continuing risks the cable breaking.

Engine failure in the hover: reduce collective for the height, release the load as soon as possible with the cable-shear pushbutton, control yaw, cyclic forward for speed and increase collective to cushion. During hoisting the pilot moves away to the right and ground crew are warned to move to the left. On ICS failure, complete the present operation or abort the mission.

sections.heading: The static-electricity warning
paragraphs: To discharge static electricity the hook must touch the ground before the cable is grasped, and any discharge cable used must be removed after the hoisting phase. If the hook hits the upper mechanical stop forcefully (failure of the automatic stop), abort the hoisting mission. On the 136 kg hoist (SUP.18) the door is opened on the pilot's order at 60 kt (111 km/h) IAS or less, heating and demisting are OFF, and power margin and parameters are checked before hoisting.

notes.title: External Load: Cargo Sling and Cargo Swing
notes.subtitle: A 750 kg Breeze Eastern sling and a 1400 kg swing on a pyramid frame — one 80 kt speed limit, non-human cargo only, and a mechanical release behind the electrical one.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual SUP.12 (Cargo sling 750 kg, Breeze Eastern P/N 17149-1) and SUP.13 / 13.1 / 13.2 (Cargo swing 1400 kg); Section 9.1 (recommendations for cargo sling operations); Section 5.5 (hover performance with external loads).

sections.heading: Two load classes
paragraphs: The cargo sling has a Breeze Eastern release unit and hook with a load sensor, allowing electrical and mechanical opening, a load indicator with zero-setting on the RH door pillar, a SLING pushbutton on the console, a release control on the cyclic grip (electrical) and a release handle under the collective (mechanical). The cargo swing is a suspended pyramid frame carrying a SIREN release unit (free rotation hook in SUP.13, fixed in SUP.13.1; SUP.13.2 uses an on-board release unit) with the same controls and a load indicator with a LD ON light.

rows: Maximum all-up weight with external load
2800 kg (6173 lb) or the maximum weight allowing OGE hover, whichever is lower
Basic manual minimum and maximum still apply

sections.heading: Operating limitations
paragraphs: The hook system is approved for external loads that are jettisonable and lifted free of land or water. Operation with a load that stays in contact with land, water or a fixed structure is not demonstrated by the manufacturer and needs approval from the responsible authority. Loads are limited to non-human external cargo. Flying with an empty net or unballasted sling is prohibited unless the operator's approved limits and procedures allow it. Two placards near the hook give the maximum sling load and the hook rigging. The pilot is responsible for setting the speed limit for the load and sling length, especially for bulky loads.

sections.heading: Emergency procedures
paragraphs: Engine failure in cruise: autorotation procedure and release the load as soon as possible. In the hover: reduce collective for the height, release the load as soon as possible, control yaw, cyclic forward, and increase collective to cushion the touchdown. During hooking the pilot moves the aircraft away to the right, and ground crew are warned to move away to the left. If electrical jettisoning fails, actuate the collective-lever mechanical release.

Cargo swing only: if the LD ON light comes on or goes out untimely, in the hover during hooking or unhooking release the load electrically and check the light; if nothing changes abort the mission, and if the status changes continue. In cruise, make a precautionary approach to the nearest helipad first.

sections.heading: Normal procedures
paragraphs: Heavy loads are delicate because a swinging load affects handling, so pilots are advised to train with gradually increasing loads. Use the shortest cable for a compact load, and keep a trailing cable or net well clear of the tail rotor when carrying no or a low load. A load attachment ring of the wrong size can cause loss or jamming of the load. In wet weather hook handlers wear thick rubber gloves, and static electricity is discharged by a conductor between the ground and the hook. Before use, SLING is switched ON, the load indicator is zeroed, and the hook is checked to open in both electrical and mechanical modes with the latch free and its return spring working. On takeoff, hook and secure the load, raise the collective very smoothly with the aircraft vertically above the load, dwell briefly with the cables tight, lift vertically and adopt an immediate forward climb attitude.

notes.title: Bambi Bucket
notes.subtitle: A 1225-litre fire-fighting bucket on the external load hook, with two speed limits and a foam option.
notes.rfmReference: AS350 B3e Flight Manual SUP.52 (Bambi Bucket model 2732S — General, Limitations, Emergency Procedures, Normal Procedures).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: The Bambi Bucket model 2732S is a fire-fighting system for carrying and releasing water or other liquids in flight, with a maximum capacity of 1225 litres. Its use needs the approval of the operational authorities; the supplement is not an operational authorisation. The bucket hangs from the external load carrying device on a shackle (SUP.13.1 or SUP.13.2) and is filled by plunging it into water. The whole load is dropped in one release. A SACKSAFOAM foam injection system is an option, with a control unit on the panel or console that only works with the cockpit lighting selector on DAY.

sections.heading: Controls
paragraphs: The SLING pushbutton on the console switches the installation on. A cyclic-grip pushbutton releases the contents of the bucket. A second cyclic-grip pushbutton electrically releases the whole load from the hook, and a trigger under the collective releases it mechanically. A load indicator shows the weight on the hook.

sections.heading: Emergency jettison
paragraphs: If the contents cannot be dumped with the cyclic-grip control, the pilot can set the bucket, full or empty, on the ground as with a sling load and ground staff release it with the load release device. If a helicopter problem requires the bucket to be jettisoned, release it with the sling electrical or mechanical release controls, ideally in a right-hand turn with a slight load factor.

sections.heading: Before takeoff
paragraphs: Check that the bucket is correctly secured and that the manufacturer's plate on the shackle and the ballast inside the bucket face forward.
